i_can: I can relate average versus instantaneous change to the idea of a limit and read and interpret limit notation.
I can estimate a limit from a graph or table.

misconceptions: Treating the function value at a point as automatically equal to the limit.
Reading a limit as a value reached rather than a value approached.
Confusing average rate of change with instantaneous rate of change.

Connect shrinking secant intervals to instantaneous change.

assessment_plan_authority.learning_target: Analyze continuity at a point and on intervals, and classify discontinuities using limits, function values, and piecewise definitions.
i_can: I can analyze continuity at a point and on intervals, and classify discontinuities using limits, function values, and piecewise definitions.
I can determine parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous.
I can justify a discontinuity classification from multiple representations.
misconceptions: Checking only whether a function value exists rather than all continuity conditions.
Confusing a removable discontinuity with a jump or infinite discontinuity.
Forgetting to compare one-sided behavior at a piecewise boundary.
modeling_applications: Determine parameter values that make a piecewise function continuous.
Justify a discontinuity classification from multiple representations.
recurring_practices: Representation connection: Use the section’s graphical/numerical/symbolic representations to support the same mathematical conclusion and explain any apparent mismatch.
Justification / conditions: Identify the mathematical condition or evidence that supports the conclusion rather than naming a rule or theorem without support.
Notation / communication: Use the section’s limit, derivative, or integral notation precisely enough that the object, point/interval, and operation are unambiguous.
Modeling: Translate between the stated situation and a mathematical model/diagram, preserving the meaning of variables, dimensions, and relationships.

General Strategy The idea of fragmenting net effects into finite sums of easily estimated small changes is not new. We used it in Section 5.1 to estimate cardiac output, volume, and air pollution. What is new is that we can now identify many of these sums as Riemann sums and express their limits as integrals. The advantages of doing so are twofold. We calculate values for the regular pieces using known formulas, then sum them to find a value for the irregular whole. This approach to problem solving was around for thousands of years before calculus came along, but it was tedious work and the more accurate you wanted to be the more tedious it became. I have a Bachelor’s degree in Physics, a Master’s degree in Astronomy, and a Ph.D. in Astronomy and Astro- physics. From 1988 to 1990 I was a mem- ber of the Peace Corps, and I taught mathematics to high school students in the Fiji Islands. Calculus is a required course in high schools there. This approach to problem solving was around for thousands of years before calculus came along, but it was tedious work and the more accurate you wanted to be the more tedious it became.
